entries.title: Mercury poach forward Maddy Westbeld from Sky
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> got poached again.</p><p>The Mercury signed Sky development player Maddy Westbeld to a rest-of-season contract Tuesday, the second time this season another team has plucked one of Chicago’s development players.</p><p>Unlike the Lynx’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/01/ahead-of-trade-deadline-skys-tyler-marsh-focused-on-team-he-has-minus-chloe-bibby" >signing of Chloe Bibby</a>, though, this one won't affect the Sky’s rotation.</p><p>Westbeld appeared in only three of her allotted 12 games this season and last played June 20 against the Wings. Injuries prevented her from carving out a role.</p><p>She entered training camp with a foot injury that initially kept her sidelined, then injured her thumb around the All-Star break and had been working her way back.</p><p>“We drafted her injured, and she came in and worked her tail off,” coach Tyler Marsh said. “She played through injury most of last year, took some time to recover over this past offseason, and then showed some spurts this year at times when she was healthy.”</p><p>Westbeld became a meaningful part of the locker room since being drafted in 2025. Marsh routinely described her as an all-time great teammate, and the two also bonded over their faith.</p><p>“She just approached it with a level of maturity that most rookies don’t,” Marsh said. “She’ll always have a special place with me and with this organization.”</p><p>The Sky technically had the right to match the Mercury’s offer and convert Westbeld to a standard contract, but they did not have the cap space to do so.</p><p>Asked whether the Sky might sign another development player for the rest of the season, Marsh said they would do “what makes sense.”</p><p>Only nine games remain, but one benefit of adding another development player is that the Sky would retain that player’s rights for next season.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: 16-year-old hospitalized after being shot by several people in West Pullman
entries.summary: <p>A 16-year-old was hospitalized after being shot in West Pullman Tuesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The teen was outside in the 11700 block of South Normal Avenue at 8:23 p.m. when several people got out of a light-colored vehicle and fired shots, police said. </p><p>The 16-year-old was shot in the left forearm and grazed on his stomach. The boy was taken to Christ Medical Center in good condition.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Tied Crosstown game between Cubs, White Sox goes into late weather delay
entries.summary: <p>A tied Crosstown tilt between the Cubs and White Sox went into a late weather delay Tuesday night at Wrigley Field.</p><p>Though it had yet to start raining in Wrigleyville, the grounds crew brought the tarp out with weather in the area following the top of the eighth inning.</p><p>The Cubs tied the game at 3 in the bottom of the seventh on an Alex Bregman two-out base hit.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Schaumburg woman hospitalized after being hit by Metra train
entries.summary: <p>A woman was hospitalized after being struck by a train in Schaumburg Tuesday afternoon, according to Metra officials.</p><p>The woman, who survived, was taken to Alexian Brothers Hospital after being hit at the Schaumburg Metra station by an outbound Milwaukee District North train, according to Metra.</p><p>The woman’s condition wasn’t known. Schaumburg’s police and fire departments didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Trains were returned to service at about 4:30 p.m., the Metra said.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Contending White Sox are ahead of schedule, and starting pitching development is struggling to keep pace
entries.summary: <p>This spring, the White Sox anticipated having what would amount to nearly a second major-league rotation at Triple-A Charlotte, with top prospects Noah Schultz, Hagen Smith, Tanner McDougal and David Sandlin all in tow and all expected to reach Chicago by midseason.</p><p>Fast-forward to mid-August, and all four have debuted for a Sox team that’s surprising everyone — including their own front office — with how quickly they’ve gone from rebuilding to competing for a division title.</p><p>But since a scuffling Schultz was optioned back to Triple-A on Aug. 8, none of these pitchers is filling slots in the rotation. In fact, since Davis Martin went on the injured list last week for a blister, no one is filling <i>two </i>slots in the five-man rotation, and the Sox were banking on veteran swingmen Erick Fedde and Jose Urquidy to handle bulk portions of glorified bullpen games for the rest of the crosstown series against the Cubs.</p><p>“We really are day-to-day here with this, just because of the usage we have had over this last series and then just not having really starters,” manager Will Venable said.</p><p>It’s a good problem for the Sox to have: a surprise contention year accelerating their major-league pitching needs. But the fact that none of their ballyhooed prospects has stepped forward to seize a rotation spot — with Opening Day starter Shane Smith and former mainstay Jonathan Cannon lingering in Triple-A — is reason to look inward.</p><p>“We’re not where I want us to be,” senior pitching adviser Brian Bannister said. “I truly believe in the next couple years we’re going to be a top-five pitching development organization. But we’re not there yet.”</p><p>Not everything related to Sox pitching should be reflexively attributed to Bannister. He learned of the Aug. 1 trade for starter Luis Castillo via social media like most everyone else. Injuries also have played a clear role in the shortfalls in starting pitching. Sandlin’s season was delayed by a month because of soreness in his back and elbow. Smith and McDougal moved to bullpen roles for the rest of 2026 because of a shoulder impingement and a flexor strain, respectively. Schultz’s struggles with another bout of tendinitis in his right knee have fueled an internal theory that the delivery mechanics that make him most effective and the ones that take stress off his lead leg are two different things.</p><p>Moreover, after the Sox struggled to land marquee position players while shopping right-hander Dylan Cease on the trade market in 2024, the last two Sox drafts have leaned heavily toward adding bats to the farm system with top picks Billy Carlson and Roch Cholowsky. Bannister endorses this approach, having seen it when he was with the 2018 Red Sox, who won the World Series.</p><p>“I’m the biggest proponent of starting with a position-player core, and this is truly how I believe to win, especially if you’re operating on a lower payroll,” Bannister said. “Your pitching will feel like it’s behind the hitting. That’s actually the healthier way to build a multi-year championship window.”</p><p>In the last two years, the Sox have installed Hawk-Eye motion tracking technology at their minor-league affiliates and incorporated biomechanical information like never before. Bannister thinks their starter shortage reflects the fickle nature of pitching development and an organization with a ways to go.</p><p>“It’s still happening right at this moment — massive overhauls behind the scenes in what our [research and development] capabilities are, and the tools that we can provide to both myself and the coaches,” he said. “We haven’t even gotten to the point where we’re actively employing the biomechanics, the Hawk-Eye data. We’ve added it to four levels, but we don’t actively have access to that data on a regular basis the way that I did at previous orgs.”</p><p>That process takes time, but the Sox’ immediate playoff ambitions are now setting the tempo.<br></p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: White Sox manager Will Venable still prioritizes platoon matchups, despite Pete-Crow Armstrong's walk-off
entries.summary: <p>When rookie left-hander <b>Hagen Smith</b> faced <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs’</a> center fielder <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> Monday night to open the 10th inning of their eventual 7-5 walk-off loss, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> win probability had dwindled to 19.2%, per <a class="Link" href="http://fangraphs.com" target="_blank" ><u>FanGraphs.com</u></a>.</p><p>But if TV analyst <b>Steve Stone</b> <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/stevestone/status/2089773130495537251?s=20" target="_blank" ><u>invoking the “Man in the Arena” passage</u></a> from president Theodore Roosevelt’s 1910 speech at the Sorbonne in Paris is any indication, those odds did but so much to soften the blowback to manager <b>Will Venable</b>’s decision to pitch to a National League MVP candidate with first base open.</p><p>“All these decisions are tough,” Venable said. “But I trust the information that we have. That’s been part of our process this entire year.”</p><p>The Sox’ information indicated that Smith, a low-slot southpaw who was tabbed to pitch because relievers <b>Grant Taylor </b>and <b>Sean Newcomb </b>were unavailable, profiled best against fellow lefties Crow-Armstrong and <b>Michael Busch</b> and should intentionally walk <b>Seiya Suzuki </b>(.976 OPS) between them. Factors such as Crow-Armstrong already sitting at 3-for-4 with a walk — or the idea of not letting the opponents’ best player beat you — were given less weight.</p><p>Despite the Sox beating low preseason expectations to lead their division in August, Venable’s adherence to platoon matchups over gut-feel decision-making has been a flashpoint.</p><p>Ironically, Venable playing the matchups also resulted in the Sox’ high point Monday. Designated hitter <b>Randal Grichuk’s </b>three-run homer in the fourth had accounted for all of their scoring entering the eighth. Nevertheless, Venable had lefty<b> Andrew Benintendi </b>pinch-hit for Grichuk against Cubs right-handed reliever <b>Ryan Zeferjahn</b> and was rewarded with a two-run homer that temporarily put the Sox back up 5-4 before <b>Nico Hoerner’s </b>RBI single in the ninth.</p><p>For the Sox, this brand of mixing and matching has become an accepted norm.</p><p>“We’ve got it pretty down now,” Benintendi told the Sun-Times. “Watch the game, watch the situations, and whoever’s in the pen throwing, if it’s a big spot, he’s gonna come in for me, or I’m going to come in for him.”</p><p><b>Step forward for Teel</b></p><p>Sox catcher <b>Kyle Teel </b>inched closer to a rehab assignment as he recovers from the sprained left ankle that has sidelined him for the last month. He completed running drills and took batting practice on the field for a second straight day Tuesday, noting that he’s able to skip without pain in his left foot.</p><p>“Today was really the first day I was able to run in a curve, like rounding bases, and not feel anything, so really, really happy about that,” Teel said.</p><p>Sox general manger <b>Chris Getz</b> said earlier this month that Teel, 24, could return to the big-league team by Sept. 1. He has been limited to a total of just 19 games this season because of hamstring, knee and ankle injuries but remains the Sox’ long-term starting catcher in the eyes of the front office.</p><p><b>Odds and ends</b></p><p>After leading the Sox with 22 homers last year, infielder <b>Lenyn Sosa</b> is no longer on a 40-man roster after the Blue Jays outrighted him to Triple-A Buffalo. The Sox traded Sosa to Toronto in April for minor-league outfielder <b>Jordan Rich</b>, who hit .233/.340/.256 for their Arizona Complex League affiliate.</p><p>† Sometimes it’s really that simple. Asked about his pinch-hit homer Monday night, Benintendi didn’t hide the ball.</p><p>“I’m not gonna lie,” he said. “I was trying to hit a homer.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module entries.title: Cubs’ trade-deadline acquisition Kevin Gausman leaves Crosstown bout early with hand cramp
entries.summary: <p>The headlining addition of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ trade-deadline haul made an early exit from Tuesday night’s tilt with the Crosstown-rival <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>.</p><p>Righty starting pitcher Kevin Gausman departed in the fifth inning, leaving with the trainer after facing two batters. The team announced his exit was forced by a cramp in his left hand.</p><p>In the fourth inning, a visit from the trainer caused a lengthy delay. He stayed in the game and struck out the final batter of the frame, then returned to start the fifth, recording a strikeout and allowing an infield single before leaving, replaced by right-hander Javier Assad.</p><p>It was an overall eventful outing for Gausman, who dealt with a lot of traffic on the bases. He walked the game’s first two batters but dodged damage in that frame. He allowed a trio of two-out singles to produce the Sox’ first run in the second inning, gave up a home run to first baseman Munetaka Murakami in the third inning and allowed a run on a couple doubles in the fourth.</p><p>Gausman finished with three runs on his tally in 4 1/3 innings, allowing seven hits and a couple walks. He struck out five and threw 86 pitches.</p><p>It was the veteran righty’s third start since joining the Cubs in the deadline deal with the Blue Jays at the beginning of the month. He was stellar in his debut, throwing seven innings of two-run ball against the Royals, then was roughed up in his second, allowing six runs to the Nationals.</p><p>Gausman has a 6.19 ERA in a Cubs uniform.</p>

entries.title: Man seriously injured in Near West Side shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was seriously injured during a shooting on the Near West Side Tuesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 23, was standing near an alley in the 600 block of West Roosevelt Road at 3:58 p.m. when a person approached him and fired shots, police said. He was shot in the chest and twice in the leg, and was taken to Stroger Hospital in serious condition.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: 13-year-old shot in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>A teen was shot while sitting inside an Englewood home Tuesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The boy, 13, was inside a residence in the 7300 block of South Emerald Avenue at 5:46 p.m. when he was shot in the leg, police said. He was taken to Comers Children’s Hospital in good condition.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>

entries.title: Pritzker signs disaster proclamation to aid recovery after months of 'relentless and unprecedented' storms
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has declared an emergency over “relentless and unprecedented” storms that have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/13/5-tornadoes-confirmed-illinois-total-25-tuesday-storms" target="_blank" ><u>spawned more than 200 tornadoes</u></a> and ravaged the state over the last two months.</p><p>The declaration would free up more state funds and resources for those recovering from the weeks of what was described by Pritzker as “severe and record-breaking weather” that brought “widespread damage from torrential downpours, flash flooding, straight-line winds and several tornadoes." </p><p>It also expedites the contract and procurement process for local governments to help speed recovery efforts.</p><p>It comes days after the governor <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/14/pritzker-flood-damage-relief-bill-homeowners-disaster-declaration-fema" target="_blank" ><u>signed a bill</u></a> allowing homeowners in the state to participate in disaster relief programs that aren’t typically covered under standard insurance policies, and less than two months after he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/30/pritzker-disaster-proclamation-tornado-flood" target="_blank" ><u>made a similar declaration</u></a> following rounds of severe storms in April and June.</p><p>"I know these storms have impacted countless Illinois families and requires we band together to help them recover,” Pritzker said in a statement.</p><p>The state’s Department of Transportation, Environmental Protection Agency and Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity will all assist the listed 15 counties in recovering from the three months of storms, as part of the order.</p><p>It includes the storms in Cook County <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/27/weather-storms-heat-wind" target="_blank" ><u>July 27</u></a> — which also affected DuPage, Lake, Vermillion and Will counties — as well as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/11/severe-weather-expected-in-chicago-area-and-other-areas-of-illinois" target="_blank" ><u>August 9-11</u></a>, which also made Champaign, DuPage, LaSalle, Tazewell and Will counties eligible for damage relief.</p><p>The first wave <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/28/storms-flooding-tornadoes-damage-worker-missing-power-outage" target="_blank" ><u>sprung up four tornadoes</u></a><u>,</u> while the most recent August wave brought <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/11/severe-weather-expected-in-chicago-area-and-other-areas-of-illinois" target="_blank" ><u>three more</u></a> to the Chicago area.</p><p>Marshall County is eligible for the storms that occurred May 16, June 10-11, as well as June 19-29. Kane County could see extra resources for storms July 2-4, while Alexander and Pulaski counties will see them for July 9-11 storms.</p><p>Champaign, Ford, Fulton, McLean and Vermillion are also eligible for resources due to the storms Aug. 13-16.</p><p>Smaller and rural communities can qualify for the Community Development Block Grant <a class="Link" href="https://prezlymail.com/c/622eb4c1-4215-4b4e-a7df-0b37a91d0426/0e18f1a2/https%3A%2F%2Fdceo.illinois.gov%2Fcommunitydevelopment%2Fpublicinfrastructuresetaside.html" target="_blank" ><u>Disaster Response</u></a> program, which is funded by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and offers up to $250,000 for local governments affected by the disaster, Pritzker’s office said. Residents have six months from the day of the declaration to apply for assistance.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/17/gary-indiana-residents-without-power-deadly-storms" >Thousands of Gary residents still without power after last week’s deadly storms</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/13/5-tornadoes-confirmed-illinois-total-25-tuesday-storms" >6 tornadoes Tuesday make record-breaking 206 total this year in Illinois</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/14/feds-to-open-disaster-loan-application-help-centers-in-wake-of-june-storms" >Feds to open disaster loan application help centers in wake of June storms</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Kamilla Cardoso has quietly become the Sky’s mainstay
entries.summary: <p>Coach Tyler Marsh realized earlier this month that he doesn’t tell Kamilla Cardoso often enough how proud he is of her.</p><p>“It’s been a tough three seasons for her here,” he said of his 25-year-old center. “Having to step into the spotlight of having to produce the way we’ve needed her to is a testament to her and her commitment to this organization.”</p><p>Cardoso indeed has dealt with every flavor of chaos since being drafted No. 3 in 2024: a coaching change after her rookie year, season-ending injuries to key teammates and the trade of fellow 2024 draftee Angel Reese.</p><p>Not to mention the persistent sense among fans and analysts that she should be further along by now.</p><p>As a lottery pick and a presumed franchise pillar, Cardoso has spent much of her young career measured against what she could become. The concern has been consistency: too many stretches when she disappeared from games, too many nights when the Sky needed more from her.</p><p>That’s changing this season.</p><p>She has become the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky’s</a> mainstay, averaging 14.8 points, 8.7 rebounds and 2.4 assists. She’s more efficient around the rim. Her playmaking continues to shine. And with Courtney Vandersloot back, she finally has a point guard who can feed her in the pick-and-roll.</p><p>“We needed her to be [a scorer] and she’s really taken that to heart,” Vandersloot told the Sun-Times. “Like ‘We’re gonna give it to you on the block and you gotta find a way to score.’ ”</p><p>So what accounts for Cardoso’s big step forward this season?</p><p>Marsh said last month, half jokingly and half seriously, that she might simply be tired of not getting her due.</p><p>There’s some evidence for the snub-fueled theory. She missed out on an All-Star selection despite being the home city’s best bet. And when ESPN ranked its top 50 WNBA players, Cardoso barely made the list at No. 40, behind players like Liberty guard Pauline Astier and Valkyries center Janelle Salaün.</p><p>Proving the doubters wrong is part of every athlete’s motivation. But Cardoso never seems particularly consumed by external perception or interested in fighting it. She hardly even argues with referees, despite Marsh’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/31/sky-coach-tyler-marsh-says-the-film-doesnt-lie-kamilla-cardoso-deserves-more-free-throws" >conviction that she doesn’t get enough calls.</a></p><p>For Cardoso, proving something to herself might be more important.</p><p>Though belief in her potential never really wavered within the Sky organization, the question was whether Cardoso believed it herself. She has acknowledged for years that she needs to play with more confidence.</p><p>“The biggest thing for Mil is you can tell she wants it now,” veteran guard Natasha Cloud said earlier this month. “I don’t know if that was there two years ago. . . . You’re starting to see her understand that if you don’t go when we’re trying to give you the [bleeping] ball, it’s a disservice to our team.”</p><p>In Tuesday’s win over the Liberty, Cardoso put the game away with a deep seal and tough finish over center Han Xu, receiving the pass from Cloud. She had started slowly but finished with 17 points and 12 rebounds.</p><p>No single grandiose explanation accounts for Cardoso’s improvement this season. She has just chipped away at it.</p><p>She stays after practice to work with her position coach. She gets extra lifts in with the veterans. The talk about wanting to be more aggressive and confident is showing up more consistently in how she plays.</p><p>The new roster has helped, too.</p><p>The 2024 and 2025 groups lacked sufficient talent, and neither gave her ideal conditions to develop offensively. She didn’t have a premier point guard or much space to operate. This year’s roster, even with its injuries, has solved a lot of those problems.</p><p>“I think rebuilding without a ‘stretch four’ was really hard for Mil,” Cloud said. “Because having two players playing in the same type of spaces, it made it hard for both of them honestly. With this freeing up for Mil . . . it could have been an All-Star season if we were winning a little bit more.</p><p>“Whether we’ve been good, whether we’ve been bad, whether the adversity, Kamilla has been solid for us.”</p><p>Solid is the perfect word to describe Cardoso’s season. And yet returning to the question of what she could become remains justified.</p><p>At 6-7 with unique mobility, she has the physical gifts to overwhelm opponents. Against Phoenix, she set a league record by making 13 consecutive field goals and scored 30 points for the first time in her career. And she has made her mark without really exploring her outside shot.</p><p>The natural questions follow.</p><p>What if she let her jumper fly more often? What if her closeouts improved? What if she cut down the silly fouls?</p><p>Those questions might eventually determine the difference between very good and great.</p><p>But they shouldn’t obscure what Cardoso already has become: a consistent, big-league threat. </p><p>Plenty of reason, in other words, for her coach to be proud.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Alex Bregman comes through in another dramatic Cubs win over White Sox, 13th Wrigley walkoff this season
entries.summary: <p>Another night, another dramatic Crosstown finish.</p><p>A night after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/17/pete-crow-armstrongs-walk-off-homer-gives-cubs-win-over-white-sox-in-back-and-forth-crosstown-clash" >Pete Crow-Armstrong’s walk-off homer</a> to give the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> an extra-inning win, it was Alex Bregman’s turn Tuesday, the team’s big free-agent signing driving in both the game-tying and game-winning runs with separate clutch hits in a 4-3 defeat of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>.</p><p>Bregman’s game-winning knock in the ninth gave the Cubs their 13th walk-off win at Wrigley Field this season.</p><p>“That’s a lot,” Cubs righty starter Kevin Gausman said. “It goes to show how special this team is, how special these guys are. They always believe in each other, and when you have that, it’s tough [to beat].”</p><p>Bregman came through twice Tuesday.</p><p>The Cubs drew back-to-back walks down a run in the bottom of the seventh before the Sox called on terrific righty reliever Grant Taylor, who struck out Crow-Armstrong and right fielder Seiya Suzuki before Bregman tied the game at 3 with a base hit to left field.</p><p>Rain came in the middle of the eighth inning and forced an hour-and-a-half delay, preventing the Sox from sending Taylor back out for another inning. In his second inning of work in the ninth, righty reliever Trevor Richards yielded a leadoff double to Cubs catcher Carson Kelly, intentionally walked Crow-Armstrong with one out and gave up another two-out knock to Bregman, who went back up the middle for the game-winner.</p><p>“You love it,” Bregman said of getting a chance in moments when the game is on the line. “Sometimes, you’re going to fail in them, but you want them every single time. Eventually, you keep putting yourself in those spots and you keep getting those opportunities, you’re going to come through. I was fortunate enough to put a good swing on it today.”</p><p>“Grant was going back out there [for the eighth], and obviously, we weren’t able to get his inning there, which puts you in a tough spot,” Sox skipper Will Venable said. “They got it right; it rained pretty heavy there, right when they thought it was going to.”</p><p>Indeed, it rained, which Cubs and Sox fans alike took as an opportunity to gather behind home plate, mostly shirtless, for some “Tarps Off” fun, twirling their shirts and singing along to “Seven Nation Army,” “Dancing Queen” and “Bear Down, Chicago Bears,” among other tunes.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">An ever-growing Tarps Off crowd is currently chanting “GREEN BAY SUCKS” while it pours rain and “Dancing Queen” blares over the Wrigley Field speakers.<br><br>Crosstown is something, folks. <a href="https://t.co/FWF3QToBM2">pic.twitter.com/FWF3QToBM2</a></p>— Vinnie Duber (@VinnieDuber) <a href="https://x.com/VinnieDuber/status/2089912645008650305?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 19, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Hours earlier, Crow-Armstrong started the scoring by picking up where he left off Monday, hitting a leadoff homer for a second straight night, and first baseman Michael Busch made it a second consecutive two-homer first for the Cubs.</p><p>But Gausman’s first home start since joining the Cubs in a deadline deal didn’t go as he’d hoped. He gave up three runs – on a trio of two-out singles in the second, on a crushed Munetaka Murakami homer in the third and a couple doubles in the fourth – before needing a lengthy visit from the trainer in the fourth and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/18/cubs-kevin-gausman-injury-hand-thumb-crosstown-white-sox-trade-deadline-rotation" >leaving early with a cramp in his left hand</a> two batters into the fifth.</p><p>“It’s pretty frustrating, to be honest, my first start here as a Cub, obviously not what I’m trying to do,” Gausman said. “It’s only the second time, I think, in my career that I left the game [with an injury]. I felt like I couldn’t keep going. I couldn’t grab my glove without [my thumb] locking up on me.”</p><p>Right-hander Javier Assad once again stepped in for an injured starter and delivered a stellar performance, throwing three scoreless innings to keep the Cubs within a run. Righty reliever Jacob Webb pitched a scoreless ninth, his 23rd consecutive scoreless appearance.</p><p>But it was Bregman’s big night, just the latest as the third baseman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/12/cubs-alex-bregman-three-homers-dansby-swanson-ryan-rolison-phil-maton-knee-injury-jackson-kent-nationals" >has heated up in the second half</a>.</p><p>“He’s a smart hitter,” Gausman said. “He knows how guys are going to pitch against him. He’s been around a long time. You mix that with the ability to change his swing to certain pitches and the mentality that he has in those big moments, he knows he’s done it before.</p><p>“It’s fun to watch.”</p>

entries.title: 2 teens critically injured in South Austin drive-by shooting
entries.summary: <p>Two teens were critically injured after they were shot in South Austin Tuesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>An 18-year-old and two 16-year-old boys were outside in the 200 block of South Central Avenue at 9:29 p.m. when a dark sedan drove past and a passenger inside fire shots, police said. </p><p>The 18-year-old was shot in his right side and one of the 16-year-olds was shot several times. Both were taken to Mt. Sinai Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>The other 16-year-old was found by officers at the scene with a graze wound to his arm and refused medical attention, police said.</p><p>Police do not have any suspects in custody. <br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Woman killed, man seriously injured in South Lawndale stabbing
entries.summary: <p>A man allegedly plunged a steak knife into a woman, killing her, before turning the weapon on himself leaving him seriously hurt late Tuesday in a South Lawndale neighborhood apartment, according to police. </p><p>No charges have been announced for the 59-year-old man, who was arrested and remained hospitalized, according to a police report.</p><p>Officers responded to a call of a person stabbed around 11:35 p.m. in the 2500 block of South Christiana Avenue and found the two suffering from stab wounds, Chicago police said. </p><p>The woman, whose age wasn’t immediately known, suffered multiple puncture wounds to her body and was pronounced dead at the scene, police said. </p><p>A 59-year-old man was also stabbed multiple times in the body and was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital where he was in serious condition, officials said. </p><p>At least one steak knife was recovered at the scene and according to the report, the 59-year-old man allegedly attacked the woman before stabbing himself. </p><p>Area 4 detectives were investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Boy, 16, fatally shot in South Lawndale drive-by
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for the vehicle responsible for a drive-by shooting that fatally wounded a 16-year-old boy late Tuesday in South Lawndale. </p><p>Around 11:10 p.m., the teen was standing outside in the 2600 block of South Hamlin Avenue when a vehicle approached and someone inside opened fire, striking him in the head and chest, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital where he was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>Police reported no arrests. </p><p>Area 4 detectives were investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: 16-year-old girl shot in foot in South Deering
entries.summary: <p>A 16-year-old girl is recovering after someone shot her in the left foot early Wednesday in the city's South Deering neighborhood on the Far South Side.</p><p>The girl, who was in good condition, could not provide much detail except that it happened around 12:35 a.m., in the 10600 block of South Bensley Avenue, police said. </p><p>She was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where she was in good condition, police said. </p><p>No arrests were made and Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Chicago should consider outcomes-based training for ex-offenders
entries.summary: <p>Earlier this year, a 39-year-old Chicago man was <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndil/pr/man-sentenced-three-years-federal-prison-illegally-possessing-loaded-handgun-chicago" target="_blank" >sentenced</a> to three years in federal prison for carrying a loaded gun on the CTA Blue Line while he was still on supervised release for a previous drug conviction. The U.S. attorney's office's news release details everything about his crime. It says nothing about the opportunities available to him when he first left prison.</p><p>The man is one of roughly <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/mayor/supp_info/ex-offender_re-entryinitiatives.html" target="_blank" >20,000 people</a> who return home to Chicago from Illinois prisons every year on top of the roughly <a class="Link" href="https://loyolaccj.org/blog/whats-driving-increases-in-the-cook-county-jail-population" target="_blank" >25,000 admissions </a>who cycle through Cook County Jail annually. Most return to a handful of neighborhoods on the South and West sides, and most come home to no job, no credentials, no savings and a record that slams doors shut.</p><p>We know what happens next. Roughly <a class="Link" href="https://idoc.illinois.gov/reportsandstatistics/factsheets.html" target="_blank" >4 in 10 </a>people released from Illinois prisons are back behind bars within three years. The <a class="Link" href="https://spac.illinois.gov/" target="_blank" >Illinois Sentencing Policy Advisory Council</a> has put a price on that revolving door — roughly <a class="Link" href="https://www.macfound.org/media/files/illinois_results_first.pdf" target="_blank" >$152,000</a> per reconviction, which factors in police, courts and corrections expenses, costs to victims and lost economic productivity. On top of that, there's <a class="Link" href="https://www.civicfed.org/iifs/blog/trends-illinois-department-corrections-spending-and-prison-population" target="_blank" >$13 billion</a> in projected costs to taxpayers over five years. Some more numbers to ponder: Cook County spends more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/criminal-justice/2024/02/07/cook-county-jail-expenses-high-despite-population-decline" target="_blank" >$130 a day</a> to hold one person at the jail. That's over $400 million a year in operating costs. Illinois spends up to <a class="Link" href="https://www.civicfed.org/iifs/blog/trends-illinois-department-corrections-spending-and-prison-population" target="_blank" >$37,000</a> annually to incarcerate one person.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8a0000" name="module-8a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>We are paying premium prices for a system that manufactures the very outcome Chicago area residents want to end, in part, because ex-offenders face difficulty looking for work.</p><p>Nationally, formerly incarcerated people face unemployment rates more than a <a class="Link" href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/03/mayor-mamdani-announces-expansion-of--next-mile-nyc--to-rikers-i" target="_blank" >dozen times</a> the U.S. average. In Illinois, <a class="Link" href="https://icjia.illinois.gov/researchhub/articles/employment-of-individuals-after-release-from-illinois-prisons--employee-characteristics-occupations-and-wages/" target="_blank" >nearly half </a>of people released from prison are still unemployed three years later. Would a second chance have changed the story of the man arrested on the Blue Line? The data says, most likely. When men and women in his position come home to real training and a good job, the revolving door stops spinning.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR266.html" target="_blank" >A </a><a class="Link" href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR266.html" target="_blank" >2013 </a><a class="Link" href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR266.html" target="_blank" >landmark study</a> by RAND found vocational training in prison raises the odds of finding work after release by 28% and cuts people's odds of going back to prison by 43%. Illinois' own <a class="Link" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2997965X.2025.2518976" target="_blank" >work-release data</a> tells the same story: Participants were 37% less likely to be reincarcerated.</p><h3>Closing the gap</h3><p>Consider a different set of statistics. The American Trucking Associations estimates the industry is short roughly <a class="Link" href="https://www.plslogistics.com/blog/truck-driver-shortage-2026/" target="_blank" >82,000 drivers</a> this year and will need to hire more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.trucking.org/news-insights/ata-releases-updated-driver-shortage-report-and-forecast" target="_blank" >a million over </a>the next decade as the workforce ages out. The Chicago area feels this reality: Job boards list more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.indeed.com/q-cdl-l-chicago,-il-jobs.html" target="_blank" >9,000 open</a> commercial truck driver jobs. The same story plays out in <a class="Link" href="https://www.indeed.com/q-diesel-technician-l-chicago,-il-jobs.html" target="_blank" >diesel technology</a>, <a class="Link" href="http://indeed.com/q-fiber-technician-l-chicago,-il-jobs.html" target="_blank" >fiber optics</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.indeed.com/q-hvac-l-chicago,-il-jobs.html" target="_blank" >heating, ventilation and air conditioning</a>. </p><p>Employers are desperate for skilled workers. But many potential workers, including ex-offenders desperate for a career, can't move forward without training.</p><p>New York City decided to close that gap — and the results should make every Chicago leader take notice. Last year, the Big Apple launched <a class="Link" href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/07/mayor-mamdani-expands-next-mile-nyc--connecting-new-yorkers-on-p" target="_blank" >Next Mile NYC</a>, a partnership between the Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice and my company, which offers ex-offenders free job training. Participants are screened, matched to a suitable trade and given individualized coaching from intake through job placement and beyond. Since launching, hundreds of ex-offenders have graduated and secured full-time jobs with annual salaries ranging from <a class="Link" href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2025/08/mayor-adams-announces-major-expansion-of-big-rig-training-progra" target="_blank" >$70,000 to $125,000</a>. To date, not a single participant has been reported rearrested.</p><p>Just as important is how the city pays for it. The contract is outcomes-based: The city pays up to $10,000 per participant who graduates and lands a job — paid only when milestones are verified, credentials obtained and jobs secured — not for seats filled or hours logged. If participants don't succeed, taxpayers don't pay. Compare that to the $152,000 cost every time someone cycles back through the justice system.</p><p>The model has also passed the hardest test in politics: surviving an administrative change. Launched under Mayor Eric Adams, the program was expanded under current <a class="Link" href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/03/mayor-mamdani-announces-expansion-of--next-mile-nyc--to-rikers-i" target="_blank" >Mayor Zohran Mamdani</a>, who brought training inside <a class="Link" href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/03/mayor-mamdani-announces-expansion-of--next-mile-nyc--to-rikers-i" target="_blank" >Rikers Island</a> last spring. Now, outreach begins before release. Jurisdictions including Massachusetts, Sacramento and Denver have since contracted for versions of the same approach.</p><p>When two mayors with different politics double down on the same program, there's no argument: Public safety comes from opportunity, not just enforcement.</p><p>It is a costly and moral failure to keep demanding bootless men and women pull themselves up by their bootstraps. Chicago can keep paying for each trip through a revolving door, or it can expand training and job opportunities for its residents who come back home.</p><p><i>Uzoma "Zo" Orchingwa is the co-founder and chief executive of Emerge Career, a workforce development technology company that trains and places current and formerly incarcerated people and other underserved populations into skilled trades careers. The Chicago native, who now resides in New York City, is also a Public Voices fellow with the OpEd Project.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-390000" name="module-390000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: Uzoma “Zo” Orchingwa

entries.title: Bears have likely Hall of Famer at core of their resurgence as guard Joe Thuney quietly leads way
entries.summary: <p>The best quality an offensive lineman can have is that no one notices him. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> left guard Joe Thuney has taken that to an extreme.</p><p>With four Pro Bowl selections and four Super Bowl rings, he’s a likely Hall of Famer, but hardly anyone thinks about him. No. 62 jerseys never sell out. He’s averse to the spotlight in every way, from politely declining all interview requests to bashfully accepting the initial NFL Protector of the Year Award.</p><p>Even his coaches overlook him during film sessions.</p><p>‘‘I’ve got to remember to watch Joe because nothing pops,’’ offensive coordinator Press Taylor said. ‘‘You’ve got to go back and really appreciate what he just did there.’’</p><p>What a crazy thing to say about someone who is probably better at his job than anyone else on the roster.</p><p>In the big picture, however, the Bears know what they have, and acquiring Thuney from the Chiefs was one of general manager Ryan Poles’ best moves in his five years on the job.</p><p>There was risk in committing $51 million over three seasons to a player in his 30s, but Thuney is worth every penny. He instantly improved the line, which bolstered the running game and made life easier for quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a>.</p><p>Review: Five stars, would sign again.</p><p>Thuney’s steadiness has mitigated the effect of the Bears’ ‘‘revolving door’’ at left tackle the last two seasons, as coach Ben Johnson put it. And when their desperation peaked last season, Thuney stepped over and played left tackle himself in the playoff game against the Rams.</p><p>There was more instability at the tackle spot Tuesday. Presumptive starter Braxton Jones did limited work, with Theo Benedet on the first team next to Thuney. Kiran Amegadjie left with an injury, and Johnson said Ozzy Trapilo is ‘‘on his own timeline’’ while recovering from a major knee injury. Jedrick Wills is in the mix, too.</p><p>It’s hectic enough that Thuney said he sometimes doesn’t immediately realize who’s next to him, though he predictably dismissed it as a non-issue.</p><p>‘‘[But] Joe would like some clarity on who he can build a rapport with,’’ Johnson said.</p><p>Nonetheless, the Bears know they can count on Thuney. As he approaches 34 in November, he’s as good, if not better, in his 30s than he was in his physical prime. He looks and sounds as though he has a lot left in the tank going into his 11th season.</p><p>‘‘You gain more experience, but your body is different than what you were at 23,’’ Thuney said. ‘‘But I just try to hold myself to a high standard, still.’’</p><p>When pressed about how much longer he wants to play, Thuney said he’s hungry for more hardware. He won two Super Bowls with the Patriots while blocking for Tom Brady, who called him ‘‘just the perfect guard,’’ and two with Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs. He said he still loves ‘‘working to get wins.’’</p><p>When Johnson sought to launch the Bears out of the listless Matt Eberflus era, he not only needed a massive upgrade on the offensive line but also a champion whose presence would remind the locker room that the Lombardi Trophy is all that matters. The guy with four rings doesn’t take a victory lap merely for winning the NFC North.</p><p>‘‘There were a lot of cool moments last year, but I don’t think anybody in this building is satisfied,’’ Thuney said. ‘‘That’s what’s so cool: There’s still a very, very strong burning hunger and desire to push more and keep going, keep improving.</p><p>‘‘There’s a lot still left to do.’’</p><p>That’s true for Thuney, too.</p><p>He has played 186 out of a possible 188 games and gone more than 11,000 snaps in his career, and he’s still dominant. In the thick August heat, he has taken only one veteran day off. He just steps in and does his work, whether anybody sees it or not.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Trump Derangement Syndrome? What about Trump's obsession with his critics?
entries.summary: <p>I agree with Donald Nauyokas’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/08/12/medicaid-safety-net-hospitals-accessible-crosswalk-signals-united-airlines-trump" >recent letter</a> stating that Donald Trump is “a leader,” in response to another reader's letter. Trump was elected twice — by slim margins — to lead our country. The one time he lost was by an even smaller margin. For good or ill, Trump leads our country, like every other president.</p><p>What <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/08/10/japanese-americans-concentration-camps-immigrants-citizenship-department-natural-resources" >Linda Hendelman’s letter</a> was really getting at by saying Trump isn't a leader, though, was what kind of leader he is. She cited several leadership qualities — integrity, honesty, accountability, responsibility, empathy, compassion. But instead of commenting on how Trump measures up on those qualities, Nauyokas pulls out the meaningless catchall phrase "Trump Derangement Syndrome," which seems to refer to anyone who criticizes Trump on anything.</p><p>But hasn’t Trump spent his entire political life having hissy fits toward anyone who disagrees with him? Doesn’t he suffer from Joe Biden and Barack Obama and Clinton (Hillary and Bill) and McCain and Cheney (and on and on) Derangement Syndromes?</p><p><i>Kevin Coughlin, Evanston</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-360000" name="module-360000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Keep the Bears in Illinois</h3><p>Dear Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a>, I am writing not only as a season ticket holder but as a lifelong passionate Bears supporter who believes this franchise represents far more than football to Illinoisans.</p><p>The possibility of the Bears leaving the state feels like a betrayal to the generations of families who have supported this team through the years. The Bears aren't just a football team; they are the NFL’s founding franchise and one of the most iconic sports organizations. For more than 100 years, Illinois fans have invested their hearts, time and loyalty. We have endured rebuild after rebuild, celebrated unforgettable moments and continued showing up because the Bears are part of our identity.</p><p>Last season was one of the most memorable experiences of my life. I attended every single game and experienced the incredible atmosphere at Soldier Field and throughout the state, including Rockford, my hometown. </p><p>Like many loyal supporters, my dad, my brother and I made a significant financial commitment during difficult economic times to continue supporting the team. Purchasing season tickets and attending every game required sacrifice, planning and dedication. But we proudly made the investment because the Bears mean so much to our family and countless Illinoisans.</p><p>That is why the idea of relocating the team across state lines is so difficult to accept. Regardless of the financial benefits, moving the Bears would sever a historic relationship built over generations and send the message that financial incentives outweigh tradition, community, loyalty and legacy.</p><p>I ask you to continue working with state and local leaders to find a solution that keeps the Bears in Illinois without placing an unfair burden on fans and taxpayers.</p><p>The Bears are more than Chicago’s team. They’re Illinois’ team. Please remember the loyal fans and do everything possible to keep the Bears where their history was built.</p><p>Remember that legacy and traditions are worth protecting.</p><p><i>Jake Graham, Rockford</i></p><h3>Egg-cellent proposal </h3><p>I can support the Bears moving to Hammond on one condition: The team has to change its name from the Bears to the Eggs.</p><p><i>Bert Rice, Edgewater</i></p><h3>Bally’s looks like a money pit </h3><p>Fran Spielman's fine article last week detailed how <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/12/ballys-permanent-casino-river-west-construction-slowdown-council-members-letter" >28 City Council members</a> sent a letter to Bally's insisting they restart construction on the entertainment portions of the casino at River West. The letter scoffs at Bally's using the video gambling terminals issue as justification for the pause and accuses the company of violating its host agreement. The City Council members could take this action, not as a roadblock, but as an opportunity.</p><p>Aside from Bally's middling record as a casino operator, the state of gambling has moved on since approval of the project. Gamblers have 24/7 access to a wider array of products than any casino can offer without leaving their homes. Bally's own disappointing revenue while at its temporary location in the Medinah Temple supports the conclusion that Chicago has happily missed its window for a profitable Downtown casino, no matter how bedecked with restaurants and concert venues. Should construction resume and Bally's open, the City Council could be forced into the position of supporting the casino, year after year, budget after budget, draining money from the city treasury to keep a bad idea afloat.</p><p>Time to scrap this parasitic enterprise and save Chicago from again mortgaging its future for the sake of illusory short-term gains.</p><p><i>Ben Huizenga, Stop Predatory Gambling Illinois, Old Irving Park</i></p><h3>City can’t get it right</h3><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2024/06/20/chicago-skyway-tolls-overcharges-motorists-privatization" >Chicago Skyway</a>. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/08/parking-meters-deal-chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-stonepeak" >parking meters</a>. Now<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/casinos-gambling/2026/08/17/ballys-chicago-casino-video-gambling-going-concern" > Bally’s</a>?</p><p>When was the last time we had a mayor who made a sound fiscal decision?</p><p><i>Mark Weiher, Lake View</i>  </p><h3>Tired of reading about racial profiling</h3><p>How many times will the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/14/traffic-stops-racial-disparities-chicago-police-department-illinois-department-transportation-driving-while-black" >Sun-Times print an article</a> about traffic stops and the "obvious" racist pattern? Please list the number of times motorists are pulled over for not committing a traffic violation or not complying with rules of the road all drivers are supposed to obey. Maybe people actually should just stop at stop signs, not turn right on red when there's a “no right turn” sign and have a valid license plate sticker or a license plate? Seems to me that a good percentage of cars on the road do not have a valid license plate sticker or even a license plate on the car at all, so why must race always be brought into it? I guess getting a valid plate sticker is just one of many forms of white privilege that this paper likes to point out. Always playing the race card is past getting old.</p><p><i>Eric Knutsen, Oak Lawn</i></p><h3></h3>
entries.author: Letters to the Editor

entries.title: Dear Abby: Calls and Messages Threaten Racy Video Leak
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> A few years ago, I started receiving mysterious phone calls from a man claiming to have in his possession videos of me performing sexual acts. I do not know where he would have gotten something like that. I changed my phone number, but somehow he got my new number and started harassing me again.</p><p>After a while, the phone calls stopped, and I haven't received one in years. Recently, I was sent a request on Facebook by a girl with no profile information who then sent me a message saying something about a video and accosting me with sexual language. I have since deleted all my social media accounts.</p><p>My question is: What if there is some video I have no knowledge of, and how do I handle it if someone decides to leak it? — <i>SCARED AND EMBARRASSED</i></p><p><b>DEAR SCARED AND EMBARRASSED:</b> What has been happening to you amounts to harassment and blackmail. That is why you should notify the police about what has been going on. I seriously doubt that there is a video. (The whole thing is probably a scam.)</p><p>If there is one and it is leaked, I recommend that you hold your head high and say to anyone who mentions it that yes, like most of the adult population in the world, you, too, have a sex life. At least then you will know who filmed it, and you can share that additional information with the authorities.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am 70. My sister is 68, and her husband is 80. He has kidney failure and needs 24/7 care. Our mother is 98. She lives independently in a condo and is mentally fully functional, but she can't cook or do housekeeping anymore. (She has cleaning help.)</p><p>My sister and I take turns making Mom warm meals, and my sister also does some light housekeeping. It takes one to two hours. My sister does this three times a week while her husband is at dialysis at a nearby facility. She also has my mother's medical and financial powers of attorney and prefers to be the one to take care of things.</p><p>I am in fairly good health but have some medical issues that may eventually make it difficult (or even impossible) to travel. This fall, I plan to go to Europe for three weeks. I would like to have someone come in to help my mom three times a week while I am gone. I would introduce this person ahead of time so that Mom could get to know them and I could show them what needs to be done.</p><p>Unfortunately, Mom doesn't want anyone other than my sister and me to care for her. My sister's plate is already more than full, so I don't want to add to it. Is it unreasonable of me to expect my mother to accept outside help? — <i>PERPLEXED IN PENNSYLVANIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR PERPLEXED:</b> Your plan is not unreasonable, but it's common for someone your mother's age to resist change. Remind her that the clock is ticking on your travel opportunities, and emphasize that the arrangement is only temporary. Tell her you will call to check in while you're away, and promise to bring back lots of photos and stories to share with her when you resume your normal caregiving routine.</p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Squirrel Flower’s new album finds its heart in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Squirrel Flower’s latest album, “Say a Prayer to the Gods of Getting Going,” reads like a travelogue of vast American highways and fleeting encounters. Written during a relentless tour schedule between 2024 and 2025, these nomadic tracks by Chicago singer-songwriter Ella O’Connor Williams were born on the road — yet their sonic heart remains very much local.</p><p>Trading the heavy distortion of 2023’s “Tomorrow’s Fire” for an ethereal folk warmth, Williams tracked much of the new material live alongside a tight-knit collective of Chicago music mainstays, a group that includes Clay Frankel (Twin Peaks), Dimitri Giannopoulos (Horse Jumper of Love) and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2025/03/27/free-range-fronted-by-gifted-chicago-songwriter-sofia-jensen-is-growing-up" target="_blank" ><u>Sofia Jensen</u></a> (Free Range).</p><div target="_blank" >Privacy Policy</a></p> </div> </form> </bsp-form> </div> </div><p>Williams captured half of the album’s tracks live at Merry Meadow, a makeshift studio in Door County, Wis., alongside co-producers Seth Engel and Jack Henry. This community spirit gave her the freedom to shift styles and find a raw, newfound trust in her own voice.</p><p>“I'd never recorded with people that lived here before,” Williams, 30, admitted. “In all of my journeying, I was, like, ‘I should try making music with people who are right in front of me instead of going somewhere else.’ It was about accepting the fact that I was still living in Chicago, even though I was traveling all the time.”</p><p>The collaborative spark grew from a cold winter songwriting retreat in Green Lake, Wis., which inspired her to break away from her traditional solo process. In May 2025, she set up a mobile recording rig in Door County to track songs for two weeks.</p><p>While the album features rock, country, and experimental moments, Williams said that producer Alex Farrar — known for his work with Wednesday and MJ Lenderman and whom she recorded with for the rest of the album — persuaded her to lean into the quieter, more spacious folk tracks.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/IU7a-68eeYw?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Squirrel Flower - Reelin [OFFICIAL MUSIC VIDEO]"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“It takes a lot of skill and restraint to make a record like that,” Williams said. “It is a challenging thing to lean into the silences and take things away instead of just laying every idea out there. Through doing that, he was encouraging me to lean into what makes my sound unique.”</p><p>That minimalist approach anchors the album’s closing song, “Weightless, Untethered.” After hearing Williams perform it, Farrar told her, “That’s the most Squirrel Flower thing I’ve ever heard.” Williams said the track’s rhythmic ebbs and flows set the tone for the entire record.</p><p>Williams, who grew up in Arlington, Mass. and attended Grinnell College in Iowa, has gravitated toward folk music since her early teens due to its extreme vulnerability, she said. Though her interests later shifted toward noise music, she returned to the genre's raw and emotional risk-taking. Capturing that feeling live required letting go of perfection. During the Wisconsin sessions, she bypassed her strict one-hour vocal warmups.</p><p>“We would start recording at 10 in the morning,” Williams said. “I would drink two cups of coffee, smoke two cigarettes, and immediately record. Doing that helped me to just really not care as much and not exercise control over my voice, which allowed it to come out in a grander way.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Miles de residentes de Gary siguen sin electricidad tras las mortales tormentas de la semana pasada
entries.summary: <p>Miles de residentes de Gary siguieron sin electricidad el lunes después de que las tormentas de la semana pasada causaran estragos en el noroeste de Indiana.</p><p>Aunque el lunes fue el primer día sin lluvia en más de una semana, varios árboles caídos aún llenaban las calles de Gary. La mayoría de los semáforos no funcionaban. Varias cuadrillas trabajaban en las líneas eléctricas y los residentes limpiaban el exterior de sus casas y sus patios.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d90000" name="module-d90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Kimberly Guajardo, que ha vivido en Gary por más de 20 años, contó que ella y su esposo estuvieron sin electricidad desde el 11 de agosto. Varios árboles grandes en su propiedad fueron derribados o perdieron ramas importantes. Se refugiaron en su sótano durante lo peor de la tormenta con su hija y sus tres nietos.</p><p>"Estamos vivos y tenemos una casa", dijo Guajardo, mientras se encontraba entre los escombros de su jardín delantero. "Conozco a mucha gente que ha perdido toda su casa. Tengo seres queridos a los que tuvieron que demolerles sus viviendas. Perdieron todo lo que tenían".</p><p>Su generador no funcionaba, pero dijeron que estaban agradecidos de tener agua corriente.</p><p>Varios residentes de Gary, incluida la hermana de Guajardo, usan agua de pozo, que requiere energía para bombear el agua por las tuberías de la casa. Su hermana ha venido cada día a recoger agua en garrafones de plástico.</p><p>Guajardo tiene una batería alimentada por paneles solares para cargar su teléfono y hieleras portátiles para mantener la comida fresca. Usan velas para iluminar su casa.</p><p>"Vivimos como en el siglo XVIII, pero nos las arreglamos", dijo.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> Algunos están ayudando a sus vecinos, mientras que otros discuten en Facebook o se pelean en las largas filas de las gasolineras.</p><p>"Tenemos que unirnos como comunidad y tratar de ayudarnos lo mejor que podamos y salir adelante", destacó Guajardo, quien nació en Chicago y creció en Alabama. "Ahora no es momento de discutir. Es momento de unirnos y hacer las cosas".</p><p>El lunes por la tarde, más de 100,000 residentes del noroeste de Indiana seguían sin electricidad, según la compañía de servicios públicos NIPSCO. Más de 300,000 personas perdieron la electricidad a causa de la tormenta.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a También seguía sin electricidad, pero tiene un generador a gasolina para mantener las luces encendidas y ver un poco de televisión por la noche. Se refugió de la tormenta en el sótano de su amigo. Cuando intentó regresar a su casa más tarde, la mayoría de las calles estaban bloqueadas por árboles y presentaban inundaciones significativas.</p><p>"Lo estoy resolviendo. Sigo comiendo, sigo teniendo agua y un techo sobre mi cabeza", dijo Betts, de 60 años. "En momentos como este, lo veo como una señal para que la gente sea un poco humilde y trate de unirse".</p><p>Betts y Guajardo no estaban seguros de cuándo volvería la electricidad. entries.title: Chicago DJ and his husband released from ICE custody, continue legal fight for asylum
entries.summary: <p>A local DJ and his husband have returned home after they were released on bond from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody last week.</p><p>Omar David Panqueva, known as DJ TUNJO, and Santiago Paez <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/08/06/suenos-dj-husband-detained-immigration-agents-midway-airport-pending-asylum-case" >were detained Aug. 2 by federal immigration agents</a> at Midway Airport, where they were set to depart on a flight to Washington, D.C., to start a series of Karol G afterparties following her tour around the country.</p><p>Panqueva performed at Sueños Music Festival in Grant Park in May, and the couple founded the Chicago-based Latin music and community event organization La Mesa Presents.</p><p>The couple, from Colombia, were released on bond Aug. 12 after proving they are not a flight risk and have no criminal history, their attorney Enrique Espinoza told the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>“The government tried to argue that they are a flight risk, but the reality is that they're not. They have fully cooperated with the government and completed all their requirements,” said Espinoza.</p><p>The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Panqueva, 26, and Paez, 27, applied for asylum after fearing persecution in Colombia because they are LGBTQ+. Despite their pending asylum case, DHS said the couple was detained for overstaying visas they obtained in 2021 that expired in 2022.</p><p>Though they’ve been released, their legal fight to remain in the country is far from over, said Espinoza. Their detention also has forced them to miss an important step in the asylum process.</p><p>The men applied for asylum through U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which determines whether an applicant meets the requirements for asylum. If that federal agency determined they did not qualify, their case would typically be referred to an immigration court, where a judge would make the final decision.</p><p>But because the men were detained, their case will now go directly to immigration court, where it could be years before they have the opportunity to appear before a judge.</p><p>Espinoza said it's become common to detain people regardless of their immigration status under the Trump administration.</p><p>“The government seems to be detaining anyone, regardless of their background and whether they have a criminal record or not,” he said. “These are not the worst of the worst, as they describe it. These are individuals that have complied with all the requirements provided by the government.”<br></p>

entries.title: Acusan a hombre de darle puñetazo a otro aficionado en el partido de los Cubs contra los Sox en Wrigley Field
entries.summary: <p>Un hombre fue arrestado y acusado de golpear a un aficionado en el juego del Clásico Crosstown del lunes por la noche en Wrigley Field, donde los Cubs vencieron a los White Sox 7-5 en entradas extras.</p><p>La pelea, que según la Policía de Chicago no está relacionada con una riña en las gradas en la octava entrada captada en un <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/DcLxaRWkZSj/" target="_blank" >video ampliamente compartido</a>, ocurrió fuera de un baño cuando el partido estaba por terminar, según registros de la corte.</p><p>La víctima, de 26 años, dijo a la policía que un hombre "lo golpeó por sorpresa" con el puño derecho, provocándole sangrado en la nariz, según un informe policial.</p><div </div><p>La policía arrestó a David Cregan, de 41 años, residente del vecindario de Archer Heights, a eso de las 10:43 p.m., y lo acusó de posesión de cocaína como delito grave y de agresión como entries.title: Illinois Tollway OKs first rate hike in nearly 15 years
entries.summary: <p>Drivers on Illinois toll roads can expect to pay 45 cents more per toll starting next year, and for the first time, there will be automatic inflation-adjusted increases every other year after that.</p><p>The Illinois Tollway board's unanimous Wednesday vote to raise fares for the first time in nearly 15 years is expected to bring in an extra $1 billion each year — money the agency says is needed to fund an expanding portfolio of construction projects. The tollway's 15-year capital plan lays out $26.5 billion in projects to maintain the system and address congestion.</p><p>The new toll rates start Jan. 1. </p><p>The hike is 45 cents per passenger vehicle, raising the current most common toll of 75 cents to $1.20 — a 60% increase. Tolls will increase roughly 30% for commercial vehicles.</p><p>In an unprecedented move, the board also voted to raise future toll rates automatically every two years, tied to the rate of inflation. The increases would begin in 2029. Increases would match changes to the Consumer Price Index but would be capped at 8%.</p><p>The hike, the first since 2012, was made possible by the state's new transit funding law, which Gov. JB Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/12/16/illinois-transit-bill-signed-pritzker" target="_blank" >signed</a> last year. The Northern Illinois Transit Authority Act raised some Chicago-area taxes to pump an extra $1.5 billion a year to state public transit, including the Chicago Transit Authority, Metra and Pace.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-hangRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-660000" name="image-660000"></a> <picture class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Illinois Tollway</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The transit law also redirected some of the sales tax on motor fuel from the state's Road Fund, typically used for road construction projects, to public transit. As a concession to labor groups, lawmakers granted the tollway permission to raise tolls to make up for that lost cash.</p><p>Even with the proposed toll rate increases, the toll rates for passenger vehicles will remain among the lowest in the nation, the tollway's Chief Financial Officer Cathy Williams told the board. After the hike, a passenger vehicle with an I-Pass will pay an average of 11 cents per mile; the national average is 16 cents per mile, she said.</p><p>Before the vote, tollway Executive Director Cassaundra Rouse said the agency held 13 public hearings in July on the potential toll hike that drew more than 1,100 people.</p><p>"We heard support. We heard concerns. And we heard important questions about affordability, about accountability, congestion and our responsibility to maintain the system that we already have," Rouse said.</p><p>Rouse said the vote was "significant" and "grounded in more than two years of analysis, a transparent public engagement process, and a shared commitment to maintaining one of the region's most important transportation systems." </p><p>The new funds will help finance everything from more lanes to reconstructed interchanges to upgrading fiber-optic cable, which the agency says it earns money from by selling access to utility companies. </p><p>Rouse emphasized that the funds will not be used for the state's public transit systems — a rumor she said had come up in the public hearings.</p><p>The Veterans Memorial Tollway, known as I-355, will see the largest investment in the agency's 15-year capital program — about $6.6 billion — by adding lanes around the interchange with I-88, reconstructing 17 miles of road near I-55, and adding lanes in each direction from Roosevelt Road to North Avenue in Glen Ellyn and Lombard.</p><p>Construction projects are also planned for the rest of the tollway's 294 miles of roads. The projects span the Reagan Memorial Tollway (I-88), the Jane Addams Memorial Tollway (I-90), the Tri-State Tollway (I-94/I-294/I-80) and the Illinois Route 390 Tollway.</p><p>The Illinois Tollway was created after World War II to help fund the construction of interstate highways around the Chicago area. The tollway's eight-person board is appointed by the governor.</p><p>Republican gubernatorial candidate Darren Bailey recently called for the state to eliminate its tolls and replace that funding with another source.</p><p>When the toll system was created in the 1950s, tollway officials said the tolls would be phased out in the 1970s after the agency's bonds had been paid off. Instead, the tollway authority made the tolls permanent to cover costs of maintenance and expansion.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/07/12/illinois-tollway-booth-transportation-tolls" target="_blank" >Illinois Tollway tears out last booths, ending age of paying with change</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/06/28/kennedy-expressway-illinois-tollway-speed-cameras-idot-pritzker" target="_blank" >On Kennedy Expressway, Illinois Tollway, no speed cameras are watching despite what signs say</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.summary: <p>This may be the golden age of Illinois high school football. The state, and specifically the Chicago area, is producing truly elite players at multiple positions and more high-quality college recruits than ever before.</p><p>There are two five-star players in the senior class according to 247Sports.com: Montini's Israel Abrams and St. Patrick's David Folorunsho. Bolingbrook's Darieon Prescott and Kam McGee of Brother Rice are five-star players in the junior class.</p><p>The senior class features six players in the nation's top 100, and the junior class has seven. Two of the top five senior quarterbacks in the country play in the area (Abrams and Hersey's Jake Nawrot).</p><p>More than 50 players in the senior class have already committed to Power Four schools.</p><p>High school football in Chicago is booming, and competition for the state's eight state titles will be fierce. The Huskies defense returns nine experienced players from a 7A quarterfinalist.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-sports/2026/05/02/herseys-jake-nawrot-who-committed-to-kentucky-is-no-5-qb-nationally-in-2027-recruiting-cycle" >Kentucky recruit Jake Nawrot, one of the best quarterbacks in the country, leads No. 10 Hersey</a></p><h3>11. Maine South</h3><p>Quarterback Jameson Purcell (Indiana) threw for more than 3,000 yards and 41 touchdowns last season. Toledo recruit Vuk Strbak heads an experienced offensive line. Senior linebacker Matthew Schlenhardt (Syracuse) is the only defensive starter back and will need to lead a young group. </p><h3>12. Glenbard West</h3><p>Senior quarterback AJ Rayford is expected to lead the Hilltoppers' offense to new heights. Tight end Brady Johnson and offensive lineman Josiah Wallace are both Northwestern recruits, and the running game is strong with Bryce Ellens and Amari Harris. The defense is young, but defensive back Jaylen McMiller is a playmaker. </p><h3>13. Providence</h3><p>Big things are possible for last season's 5A runners up. Broden Mackert and Brayden McKay combined for 2,556 yards rushing yards and 35 TDs last season. Offensive lineman Bryce Tencza returns to lead that charge, and junior Dominic Vita is one of the area's most physically imposing quarterbacks. </p><h3>14. Geneva</h3><p>The Vikings should have a major rebound year behind quarterback Ben Peterson and receiver Bennett Konkey (Illinois). Most of last season's starters return on offense, and four are back on defense. </p><h3>15. St. Rita</h3><p>Running back Brandon Johnson Jr. (Lindenwood) will benefit from a strong offensive line. Keep an eye on defensive lineman Ohimai Ozolua (Michigan State), a transfer from Romeoville.</p><h3>16. Barrington</h3><p>Lamar Osterhues is one of the state's most effective running backs, and the Broncos return 10 starters from a team that advanced to the 8A quarterfinals last season.</p><h3>17. York</h3><p>The Dukes could have one of the area's strongest defenses, with eight starters returning led by defensive end Owen Roberts (Purdue). Senior quarterback Zack Assaad picked up valuable experience last season.</p><h3>18. Lincoln-Way East</h3><p>The Griffins lost a ton from last year, but coach Rob Zvonar's program has always reloaded quickly. Mason Halliman (Illinois) will lead a strong offensive line that should provide some stability. Safety Charlie Palmer and linebacker Colton Zvonar lead a lot of new faces on defense.</p><h3>19. Kankakee</h3><p>Phillip Turner is healthy after missing the playoffs last year, and the senior quarterback could be one of the season's breakout stars. He's already accounted for 40 TDs in his career. The defense should be strong.</p><h3>20. Downers Grove North</h3><p>The core group that led to impressive success over the past few seasons has graduated, but the offensive line remains strong and quarterback Kevin Jay, tight end Jacob Vroman and linebacker Baker Glomb are impact players. </p><h3>21. Prospect</h3><p>Quarterback Jackson Cacini (EIU) and running back Matthew Donnelly head an explosive experienced offense and five starters return from last season's effective defense. </p><h3></h3><h3>22. Carmel</h3><p>Trae Taylor moved on but a load of talent remains, led by lineman Wyatt VanBoening, linebacker Jameer Miles and dynamic junior running backs Jaquel Edmonds and Jorden Moore. </p><h3>23. Sandburg</h3><p>Last year's success was a burst of confidence for the program, and the offense is experienced with quarterback Sean Ruisz, running back Quinn Durkin and receiver Lucas Matykiewicz.</p><h3>24. Fenwick</h3><p>Iowa recruit Jake Thies is a force all over the field, but the defending 6A champs will depend on a lot of new faces. Senior Jimmy Bonakdar is back from an injury and should be a major contributor.</p><h3>25. Lyons</h3><p>Ten starters return from a second-round playoff team, including running back EJ Kuhlman and tight end Owen Matela (Miami Ohio).<br></p>
